title: Φοίνικος λιταί
about: Phoenix, the old man whom Achilles has just asked to stay the night, breaks the silence in tears. He will not be left behind: Peleus sent him with the boy Achilles to teach him words and deeds, and he tells how he fled his father’s curse, was taken in by Peleus, and brought Achilles up on his own knees. He asks Achilles to master his great spirit, since even the gods can be turned. Prayers, the daughters of Zeus, come limping behind Bewilderment and heal what she harms, and Zeus lets her follow whoever rejects them. Agamemnon now offers gifts and has sent the best of the Argives, so that Achilles’ anger was blameless until now. As a precedent Phoenix tells of Meleager at Calydon: the boar sent by Artemis, the war of the Curetes and the Aetolians, and Meleager lying in anger beside his wife while every plea and every gift is refused, until she describes the fall of a town and he goes out and saves them, but without the gifts that had been promised. Phoenix ends by telling Achilles to go while the gifts are on offer, or lose his honour even if he drives the war away.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ
μῦθον ἀγασσάμενοι·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then all became still in silence,
in wonder at the speech;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all fell hushed and silent, amazed at his speech;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ … σιωπῇ is a formula, ‘so he spoke, and they all became still in silence’, which also stands at 3.95; it says that Achilles’ refusal has left the room speechless. ἀγασσάμενοι, from ἀγάομαι, can mean ‘be amazed at’ or ‘be indignant at’; the next unit gives the reason for the silence, and ‘amazed’ is the sense that suits it. μῦθον is the object, ‘the speech’, that is, the whole of Achilles’ answer. The edition begins a new paragraph here.

sentences.t: μάλα γὰρ κρατερῶς ἀπέειπεν·
sentences.l: for very strongly he had refused;
sentences.i: for he had refused with great force.
sentences.n: γάρ ‘for’ gives the reason for the silence. ἀπέειπεν is the aorist of ἀπεῖπον ‘refuse’, the verb that gives ἀπόειπε at 1.515, and it is rendered as a pluperfect (‘had refused’) because the refusal lies before the silence. κρατερῶς ‘strongly, with force’ is the adverb of κρατερός.

sentences.t:
ὀψὲ δὲ δὴ μετέειπε γέρων ἱππηλάτα Φοῖνιξ
δάκρυ’ ἀναπρήσας·
sentences.l:
But late indeed spoke among them the old man, horse-driver Phoenix,
tears bursting forth;
sentences.i: At last Phoenix, the old horse-driver, spoke among them, bursting into tears;
sentences.n: ὀψὲ δὲ δὴ μετέειπε is a whole-line speech introduction, ‘but late indeed spoke among them’, which is used at 7.399 of Diomedes. γέρων ἱππηλάτα ‘old man, horse-driver’ is a stock pair, as for Nestor in the Odyssey and for Peleus at 7.125, and it is translated every time. Phoenix is the envoy whom Achilles has just asked to stay the night. δάκρυ’ ἀναπρήσας: the verb ἀναπρήθω is rare and its root is not certain, and ‘bursting into tears’ (tears ‘bursting forth’) is the traditional sense.

sentences.t: περὶ γὰρ δίε νηυσὶν Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.l: for greatly he feared for the ships of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: for he was deeply afraid for the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: δίε is the past tense of δίω ‘fear’, without augment, and νηυσίν is the epic dative plural, ‘for the ships’. περί is best taken as an adverb, ‘exceedingly’, though it can also be read with δίε as a tmesis (a preverb standing apart from its verb). Phoenix weeps because he fears for the camp; his speech begins in the next unit.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὲν δὴ νόστόν γε μετὰ φρεσὶ φαίδιμ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ
βάλλεαι, οὐδέ τι πάμπαν ἀμύνειν νηυσὶ θοῇσι
πῦρ ἐθέλεις ἀΐδηλον, ἐπεὶ χόλος ἔμπεσε θυμῷ,
sentences.l:
“If now a homecoming, glorious Achilles, in your wits
you are casting, and not at all to ward off from the swift ships
the destroying fire do you wish, since anger has fallen on your heart,
sentences.i: “If you are set on going home, glorious Achilles, and do not wish at all to keep the destructive fire from the swift ships, since anger has fallen on your heart,
sentences.n: The edition prints no quotation marks, so they are ours. εἰ μὲν δή opens a condition that runs on into the question of the next unit. βάλλεαι is the second person of the middle of βάλλω, with the epic ending -εαι (= Attic -ῃ); νόστον … μετὰ φρεσὶ βάλλεαι is ‘you are casting a homecoming in your wits’, that is, you are planning to go home. ἀμύνειν takes the dative νηυσὶ θοῇσι ‘from the swift ships’; πῦρ ἀΐδηλον is the enemy’s fire, and ἀΐδηλος is of disputed sense (‘destroying’ or ‘unseen’), the house choice being ‘destroying’ in the literal line and ‘destructive’ in the free one. ἔμπεσε is the aorist of ἐμπίπτω ‘fall upon’, without augment. φαίδιμ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ is a stock vocative, ‘glorious Achilles’.

sentences.t:
πῶς ἂν ἔπειτ’ ἀπὸ σεῖο φίλον τέκος αὖθι λιποίμην
οἶος;
sentences.l:
how then, away from you, dear child, here would I be left
alone?
sentences.i: how then could I be left behind here, dear child, away from you, alone?
sentences.n: πῶς ἂν … λιποίμην is a question with ἄν and the optative, ‘how could I be left?’, and it is the main clause of the condition in the last unit. λιποίμην is the aorist middle optative of λείπω, whose middle means ‘be left behind’. σεῖο is the epic genitive of σύ (= σοῦ) after ἀπό. φίλον τέκος ‘dear child’ is the old man’s way of addressing Achilles. οἶος ‘alone’ closes the question, and the rest of the line starts the next unit.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δέ μ’ ἔπεμπε γέρων ἱππηλάτα Πηλεὺς
ἤματι τῷ ὅτε σ’ ἐκ Φθίης Ἀγαμέμνονι πέμπε
νήπιον οὔ πω εἰδόθ’ ὁμοιΐου πολέμοιο
οὐδ’ ἀγορέων, ἵνα τ’ ἄνδρες ἀριπρεπέες τελέθουσι.
sentences.l:
To you he sent me, the old man, horse-driver Peleus,
on that day when from Phthia to Agamemnon he sent you,
a child, not yet knowing war common to all
nor assemblies, where men become outstanding.
sentences.i: Peleus, the old horse-driver, sent me along with you on the day when he sent you from Phthia to Agamemnon, a mere child who knew nothing yet of the war that is common to all, nor of assemblies, where men become outstanding.
sentences.n: σοὶ δέ μ’ ἔπεμπε is ‘to you he sent me’, the dative σοί being ‘along with you’. The second line, ἤματι τῷ ὅτε σ’ ἐκ Φθίης Ἀγαμέμνονι πέμπε, also stands at 9.253, where Odysseus quotes Peleus’ charge; πέμπε is the unaugmented form of ἔπεμπε. νήπιον agrees with σε and means a child here, simply too young; elsewhere the word is ‘foolish’. εἰδόθ’ is the perfect participle εἰδότα ‘knowing’, with the genitives ὁμοιΐου πολέμοιο and ἀγορέων, ‘knowing nothing of war … nor of assemblies’. ὁμοίϊος is of uncertain sense (‘common to all’, ‘levelling’), and ‘common to all’ is the house reading. ἀγορέων is the genitive plural of ἀγορή ‘assembly’; ἀριπρεπέες is ‘outstanding’, and τελέθουσι ‘become, are’.

sentences.t:
τοὔνεκά με προέηκε διδασκέμεναι τάδε πάντα,
μύθων τε ῥητῆρ’ ἔμεναι πρηκτῆρά τε ἔργων.
sentences.l:
For that reason he sent me forth to teach all these things,
to be of words a speaker and of deeds a doer.
sentences.i: That was why he sent me out, to teach you all this: to be a speaker of words and a doer of deeds.
sentences.n: τοὔνεκα (τοῦ ἕνεκα) ‘for that reason’ looks back to 440–441: Achilles knew neither war nor assemblies. προέηκε is the aorist of προΐημι ‘send forth’, and διδασκέμεναι is the epic infinitive in -μεναι (= διδάσκειν), with τάδε πάντα ‘all this’. ἔμεναι (= εἶναι) has two predicate accusatives, ῥητῆρα ‘speaker’ and πρηκτῆρα ‘doer’, each with its genitive, μύθων and ἔργων: the pair, words and deeds, is Phoenix’s summary of his teaching.

sentences.t:
ὡς ἂν ἔπειτ’ ἀπὸ σεῖο φίλον τέκος οὐκ ἐθέλοιμι
λείπεσθ’, οὐδ’ εἴ κέν μοι ὑποσταίη θεὸς αὐτὸς
γῆρας ἀποξύσας θήσειν νέον ἡβώοντα,
sentences.l:
So then, away from you, dear child, I would not wish
to be left, not even if a god himself were to promise me,
having scraped off old age, to make me young and in youthful prime,
sentences.i: So I could never wish to be left behind away from you, dear child, not even if a god himself were to promise to scrape off my old age and make me young and in youthful prime,
sentences.n: ὡς ἂν … οὐκ ἐθέλοιμι answers the question of 437: ὡς ‘so, in that way’ with ἄν and the optative, ‘so I would not wish’. λείπεσθ’ is the infinitive λείπεσθαι ‘be left behind’. οὐδ’ εἴ κεν … ὑποσταίη is a supposition, ‘not even if … should promise’ (ὑφίσταμαι, aorist optative, ‘undertake, promise’), with the future infinitive θήσειν ‘to make’. ἀποξύσας ‘having scraped off’ pictures old age as something scraped away like a skin. νέον ἡβώοντα are accusatives agreeing with an unspoken με ‘me’: ‘young, in youthful prime’ (ἡβώοντα is the uncontracted participle of ἡβάω).

sentences.t:
οἷον ὅτε πρῶτον λίπον Ἑλλάδα καλλιγύναικα
φεύγων νείκεα πατρὸς Ἀμύντορος Ὀρμενίδαο,
sentences.l:
such as when first I left Hellas of the fair women,
fleeing the quarrels of my father Amyntor, Ormenus’-son,
sentences.i: such as I was when I first left Hellas of the fair women, running from the quarrels of my father Amyntor, son of Ormenus,
sentences.n: οἷον ‘such as’ qualifies the young man of 446: Phoenix would not leave Achilles even if made as young as he was when he fled. Ἑλλάς here is a district, not the whole of Greece, and the house rendering is ‘Hellas of the fair women’ (καλλιγύναικα, as at 2.683). Ἀμύντορος is the name of Phoenix’s father, and Ὀρμενίδαο is a patronymic with the epic genitive -αο (= -ου), ‘son of Ormenus’. νείκεα is the uncontracted plural of νεῖκος ‘quarrel’.

sentences.t:
ὅς μοι παλλακίδος περιχώσατο καλλικόμοιο,
τὴν αὐτὸς φιλέεσκεν, ἀτιμάζεσκε δ’ ἄκοιτιν
μητέρ’ ἐμήν·
sentences.i: who was incensed with me over a fair-haired concubine, whom he himself loved, while he dishonoured his wife, my mother.
sentences.n: ὅς is the relative ‘who’, Amyntor. περιχώσατο, the aorist of περιχώομαι ‘be very angry about’, takes the genitive παλλακίδος ‘over a concubine’; χώομαι is the verb of ‘incensed’ in this story. φιλέεσκεν and ἀτιμάζεσκε are iterative imperfects in -εσκ-, ‘used to love’, ‘used to dishonour’, which show a habit; ἄκοιτιν μητέρ’ ἐμήν ‘wife, my mother’ is a plain apposition. καλλικόμοιο ‘fair-haired’ is the same word as in Helen of the fair hair in the Odyssey.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ αἰὲν ἐμὲ λισσέσκετο γούνων
παλλακίδι προμιγῆναι, ἵν’ ἐχθήρειε γέροντα.
sentences.l:
but she always kept begging me, at my knees,
to lie first with the concubine, that she might hate the old man.
sentences.i: but she, my mother, kept begging me at my knees to lie with the concubine first, so that the woman would come to hate the old man.
sentences.n: ἣ is ‘she’, the mother; λισσέσκετο is another iterative imperfect, ‘kept begging’, and γούνων is the genitive of the knees at which one pleads. προμιγῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of προμίγνυμι ‘mix first with’, here ‘lie with’, and it takes the dative παλλακίδι. ἵν’ ἐχθήρειε is a purpose clause with the optative of ἐχθαίρω ‘hate’; its subject is the concubine, and γέροντα ‘old man’ is Amyntor.

sentences.t: τῇ πιθόμην καὶ ἔρεξα·
sentences.l: Her I obeyed, and I did it;
sentences.i: I obeyed her and did it.
sentences.n: τῇ is the article as a pronoun, in the dative with πιθόμην, ‘I obeyed her’ (πείθομαι takes the dative); πιθόμην is the aorist without augment. ἔρεξα is the aorist of ῥέζω ‘do’, and the deed, lying with the concubine, is left unsaid. The ano teleia leads into what his father did.

sentences.t:
πατὴρ δ’ ἐμὸς αὐτίκ’ ὀϊσθεὶς
πολλὰ κατηρᾶτο, στυγερὰς δ’ ἐπεκέκλετ’ Ἐρινῦς,
μή ποτε γούνασιν οἷσιν ἐφέσσεσθαι φίλον υἱὸν
ἐξ ἐμέθεν γεγαῶτα·
sentences.l:
and my father, at once suspecting it,
much cursed, and hateful Erinyes he called upon,
that never upon his own knees would sit a dear son
begotten from me;
sentences.i: and my father, guessing it at once, cursed me bitterly and called on the hateful Erinyes, praying that no dear son born of me should ever sit upon his knees;
sentences.n: ὀϊσθείς is the aorist passive participle of ὀΐομαι ‘suspect, guess’. κατηρᾶτο is the imperfect of καταράομαι ‘curse’, and ἐπεκέκλετ’ the aorist of ἐπικέλομαι ‘call upon’; the Ἐρινύες are the avenging spirits of a wronged parent. μή ποτε … ἐφέσσεσθαι gives the content of the curse: an infinitive of the verb ‘sit upon’ (ἐφέζομαι), with the accusative φίλον υἱὸν ‘a dear son’ as its subject. γούνασιν οἷσιν is ‘upon his own knees’, and οἷσιν is the possessive ὅς (‘his own’), not the relative. ἐξ ἐμέθεν (ἐμέθεν = ἐμοῦ) is ‘from me’, and γεγαῶτα is the perfect participle of γίγνομαι ‘born, begotten’.

sentences.t:
θεοὶ δ’ ἐτέλειον ἐπαρὰς
Ζεύς τε καταχθόνιος καὶ ἐπαινὴ Περσεφόνεια.
sentences.l:
and the gods fulfilled the curses,
Zeus beneath the earth and grim Persephone.
sentences.i: and the gods fulfilled his curses, Zeus of the underworld and grim Persephone.
sentences.n: ἐτέλειον is the imperfect of τελέω in its epic form (= ἐτέλουν), ‘were fulfilling’, with ἐπαράς ‘curses’ as its object. Ζεὺς καταχθόνιος ‘Zeus beneath the earth’ is Zeus as ruler of the dead; ἐπαινή, ‘grim’ (traditionally ‘dread, awful’; the exact sense is not certain), is the stock epithet of Persephone. The edition omits 9.458–461, which it gives only in its apparatus, so its numbering jumps from 457 to 462 in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἐμοὶ οὐκέτι πάμπαν ἐρητύετ’ ἐν φρεσὶ θυμὸς
πατρὸς χωομένοιο κατὰ μέγαρα στρωφᾶσθαι.
sentences.l:
Then no longer at all was my heart restrained in my wits
from going to and fro through the halls of my angry father.
sentences.i: Then my heart within me could no longer be held back from going to and fro through the halls of my angry father.
sentences.n: The edition has no 9.458–461, so the numbering goes straight from 457 to 462. ἔνθα ‘then, at that point’ marks the turn. ἐρητύετ’ is the imperfect passive of ἐρητύω ‘hold back’, with ἐν φρεσί ‘in the wits’ and an infinitive of what he was held from, στρωφᾶσθαι ‘to turn about, go to and fro’. κατὰ μέγαρα is ‘through the halls’, and χωομένοιο is the epic genitive agreeing with πατρός, ‘my father, still incensed’.

sentences.t:
ἦ μὲν πολλὰ ἔται καὶ ἀνεψιοὶ ἀμφὶς ἐόντες
αὐτοῦ λισσόμενοι κατερήτυον ἐν μεγάροισι,
sentences.l:
Truly, often kinsmen and cousins, being round about,
beseeching me there, kept holding me back in the halls,
sentences.i: Truly, my kinsmen and cousins, gathered all around, begged me often and held me back there in the halls,
sentences.n: ἦ μέν ‘truly’ introduces a strong assertion. ἔται is the plural of ἕτης ‘kinsman’ and ἀνεψιοί are ‘cousins’; ἀμφὶς ἐόντες ‘being round about’ has the epic participle ἐόντες (= ὄντες). αὐτοῦ is an adverb, ‘on the spot, there’, and κατερήτυον is the imperfect of κατερητύω ‘hold back’, the compound of the verb of 462. πολλά is adverbial, ‘much, often’.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δὲ ἴφια μῆλα καὶ εἰλίποδας ἕλικας βοῦς
ἔσφαζον, πολλοὶ δὲ σύες θαλέθοντες ἀλοιφῇ
εὑόμενοι τανύοντο διὰ φλογὸς Ἡφαίστοιο,
sentences.l:
and many stout flocks and rolling-gaited, crumple-horned cattle
they slaughtered, and many pigs, abundant with fat,
being singed, were stretched out through the flame of Hephaestus,
sentences.i: They slaughtered many stout flocks and cattle of rolling gait and crumpled horn, and many pigs, abounding in fat, were stretched out to be singed through the flame of Hephaestus,
sentences.n: ἴφια μῆλα ‘stout flocks’ and εἰλίποδας ἕλικας βοῦς ‘rolling-gaited, crumple-horned cattle’ are fixed phrases and are translated as the Odyssey has them. ἔσφαζον is the imperfect of σφάζω ‘slaughter’, and its subject, the kinsmen, is understood from the last unit. σύες is the plural of σῦς ‘pig’; θαλέθοντες, from θαλέθω ‘flourish’, with the dative ἀλοιφῇ means ‘abounding in fat’, from the same root as θαλερός ‘abundant’. εὑόμενοι ‘being singed’ (εὕω) and τανύοντο ‘were stretched out’ show the carcasses held in the fire; Ἡφαίστοιο ‘of Hephaestus’ stands for the fire itself, as at 2.426.

sentences.t: πολλὸν δ’ ἐκ κεράμων μέθυ πίνετο τοῖο γέροντος.
sentences.l: and much wine from the jars of that old man was drunk.
sentences.i: and much wine was drunk from that old man’s jars.
sentences.n: πολλόν is the neuter ‘much’ (= πολύ), agreeing with μέθυ ‘wine’, a poetic word. ἐκ κεράμων ‘from jars’ (κέραμος, a clay jar); τοῖο γέροντος ‘of that old man’ is Amyntor, Phoenix’s father, and τοῖο is the epic genitive of the article as a pronoun (= τοῦ). The kinsmen are feasting at the father’s expense to keep the son in the house.

sentences.t: εἰνάνυχες δέ μοι ἀμφ’ αὐτῷ παρὰ νύκτας ἴαυον·
sentences.l: Nine nights long, around me myself, through the nights they slept;
sentences.i: For nine nights they slept all around me, night after night;
sentences.n: εἰνάνυχες ‘for nine nights’ is an adverbial adjective, nine-night. ἀμφ’ αὐτῷ is ‘around me myself’, the dative μοι being ethic and αὐτῷ the man they guard. παρὰ νύκτας is ‘night by night, through the nights’, and ἴαυον is the imperfect of ἰαύω ‘sleep, pass the night’. The next unit says how the watch was kept.

sentences.t:
οἳ μὲν ἀμειβόμενοι φυλακὰς ἔχον, οὐδέ ποτ’ ἔσβη
πῦρ, ἕτερον μὲν ὑπ’ αἰθούσῃ εὐερκέος αὐλῆς,
ἄλλο δ’ ἐνὶ προδόμῳ, πρόσθεν θαλάμοιο θυράων.
sentences.l:
They, taking turns, kept watches, and never went out
a fire, one beneath the portico of the well-fenced court,
and the other in the fore-house, in front of the doors of the chamber.
sentences.i: They kept watch in turns, and the fire never went out, one under the portico of the well-fenced courtyard, the other in the vestibule, in front of the doors of the chamber.
sentences.n: ἀμειβόμενοι ‘taking turns’ (ἀμείβομαι ‘exchange’) goes with φυλακὰς ἔχον ‘kept watch’, and ἔχον is unaugmented. πῦρ is the subject of ἔσβη ‘went out’ (the aorist of σβέννυμι, here intransitive). There were two fires, ἕτερον … ἄλλο ‘one … the other’: one under the αἴθουσα ‘portico’ of the courtyard (εὐερκής ‘well-fenced’), and one in the πρόδομος, the room before the chamber (θάλαμος).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ δεκάτη μοι ἐπήλυθε νὺξ ἐρεβεννή,
καὶ τότ’ ἐγὼ θαλάμοιο θύρας πυκινῶς ἀραρυίας
ῥήξας ἐξῆλθον, καὶ ὑπέρθορον ἑρκίον αὐλῆς
ῥεῖα, λαθὼν φύλακάς τ’ ἄνδρας δμῳάς τε γυναῖκας.
sentences.l:
But when at last the tenth murky night came upon me,
then I, the doors of the chamber closely fitted
breaking, went out, and leapt over the fence of the court
easily, unnoticed by the guards, men, and by the maidservants, women.
sentences.i: But when the tenth night came upon me, a murky night, then I broke the closely fitted doors of the chamber and went out, and I leapt over the fence of the courtyard with ease, unnoticed by the men who kept watch and by the maids.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή … καὶ τότε is the pattern ‘but when at last … then’. δεκάτη νὺξ ἐρεβεννή is ‘the tenth night, murky’ (ἐρεβεννός ‘murky’). πυκινῶς ἀραρυίας is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’ with the adverb ‘closely’, agreeing with θύρας ‘doors’; ῥήξας is the aorist participle of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’. ὑπέρθορον is the aorist of ὑπερθρῴσκω ‘leap over’, with ἑρκίον αὐλῆς ‘the fence of the court’. λαθών (from λανθάνω) takes the accusative, ‘unnoticed by’, and ἄνδρας and γυναῖκας in apposition give the sex of the φύλακας and δμῳάς. ῥεῖα is ‘easily’.

sentences.t:
φεῦγον ἔπειτ’ ἀπάνευθε δι’ Ἑλλάδος εὐρυχόροιο,
Φθίην δ’ ἐξικόμην ἐριβώλακα μητέρα μήλων
ἐς Πηλῆα ἄναχθ’·
sentences.i: Then I fled far off through spacious Hellas, and came to Phthia, rich-soiled mother of flocks, to the lord Peleus;
sentences.n: φεῦγον is an unaugmented imperfect, ‘I fled’. ἀπάνευθε is ‘far off’, and εὐρυχόροιο ‘spacious’ (εὐρύς + χῶρος) has the epic genitive -οιο, here again of Hellas the district. ἐξικόμην is the aorist of ἐξικνέομαι ‘arrive at’ and takes the accusative Φθίην; ἐριβώλακα ‘rich-soiled’ and μητέρα μήλων ‘mother of flocks’ praise Phthia as a land of sheep. ἄναχθ’ is ἄνακτα, the accusative of ἄναξ ‘lord’, in apposition to Πηλῆα, with ἐς ‘to’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δέ με πρόφρων ὑπέδεκτο,
καί μ’ ἐφίλησ’ ὡς εἴ τε πατὴρ ὃν παῖδα φιλήσῃ
μοῦνον τηλύγετον πολλοῖσιν ἐπὶ κτεάτεσσι,
sentences.l:
and he received me ready-minded,
and loved me as if a father were to love his own son,
an only one, late-born, with many possessions,
sentences.i: and he received me with a ready mind, and loved me as a father loves his own son, an only child, born late, with many possessions to come to him,
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Peleus, and the article is a pronoun; πρόφρων is ‘ready-minded’. ὡς εἴ τε … φιλήσῃ is ‘as if a father should love’, with the aorist subjunctive, and ὃν is the possessive ὅς ‘his own’. τηλύγετος is rendered ‘late-born’ everywhere, though its sense is not certain. πολλοῖσιν ἐπὶ κτεάτεσσι is ‘over many possessions’; with the only son, the sense is that he will inherit them. κτεάτεσσι is the epic dative plural of κτέατα.

sentences.t: καί μ’ ἀφνειὸν ἔθηκε, πολὺν δέ μοι ὤπασε λαόν·
sentences.l: and he made me rich, and gave me many people;
sentences.i: and made me rich and gave me a numerous people;
sentences.n: ἀφνειόν ‘rich’ is the Odyssey’s rendering and is a predicate: ‘he made me rich’. ὤπασε is the aorist of ὀπάζω ‘grant, give as a following’, and πολὺν … λαόν is ‘a large people’, the subjects Phoenix will rule in the next line. μοι with ὤπασε is ‘to me’.

sentences.t: ναῖον δ’ ἐσχατιὴν Φθίης Δολόπεσσιν ἀνάσσων.
sentences.l: and I dwelt on the edge of Phthia, ruling over the Dolopes.
sentences.i: and I lived on the edge of Phthia, ruling the Dolopes.
sentences.n: ναῖον is the unaugmented imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell’, and ἐσχατιήν ‘the furthest part, the edge’ is an accusative of the place. ἀνάσσων ‘ruling’ takes the dative Δολόπεσσιν, the epic dative plural of the Dolopes, the people over whom Peleus set him.

sentences.t:
καί σε τοσοῦτον ἔθηκα θεοῖς ἐπιείκελ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ,
ἐκ θυμοῦ φιλέων, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἐθέλεσκες ἅμ’ ἄλλῳ
οὔτ’ ἐς δαῖτ’ ἰέναι οὔτ’ ἐν μεγάροισι πάσασθαι,
sentences.l:
And you I made so great, Achilles, resembling the gods,
loving you from my heart, since you would not with another
either go to a feast or taste food in the halls,
sentences.i: And I made you as great as you are, Achilles, like the gods, loving you from my heart, since you would not go with anyone else to a feast or eat in the halls,
sentences.n: τοσοῦτον ἔθηκα is ‘I made you so great (as you are now)’: Phoenix claims to have brought him up. θεοῖς ἐπιείκελε ‘resembling the gods’ is a stock vocative and is translated every time; ἐπιείκελος takes the dative (as at 4.394, with the immortals). ἐκ θυμοῦ φιλέων is ‘loving from the heart’. ἐθέλεσκες is an iterative imperfect, ‘you would never be willing’; ἅμ’ ἄλλῳ is ‘with another’. πάσασθαι is the aorist infinitive of πατέομαι ‘taste, eat’.

sentences.t:
πρίν γ’ ὅτε δή σ’ ἐπ’ ἐμοῖσιν ἐγὼ γούνεσσι καθίσσας
ὄψου τ’ ἄσαιμι προταμὼν καὶ οἶνον ἐπισχών.
sentences.l:
until I, upon my own knees having seated you,
should fill you with food, carving it first, and holding the wine to you.
sentences.i: until I sat you on my knees and fed you full, cutting up the food first, and held the wine to you.
sentences.n: πρίν γ’ ὅτε δή is ‘until the time when’. ἄσαιμι, the aorist optative of ἄω ‘satiate’, is the optative of a repeated event in the past, ‘until I would fill you’; ἐπ’ ἐμοῖσιν … γούνεσσι is ‘upon my knees’ (ἐμοῖσιν the possessive, γούνεσσι the epic dative plural), the scene that the curse of 455 had forbidden with a son of his own. ὄψου is the genitive after ἄσαιμι, ‘with food’; ὄψον is the prepared dish eaten with bread. προταμών ‘carving first’ is from προτέμνω, and ἐπισχών ‘holding to’ from ἐπέχω.

sentences.t:
πολλάκι μοι κατέδευσας ἐπὶ στήθεσσι χιτῶνα
οἴνου ἀποβλύζων ἐν νηπιέῃ ἀλεγεινῇ.
sentences.l:
Often you wetted the tunic on my chest
spurting out the wine in your grievous infancy.
sentences.i: Many a time you soaked the tunic on my chest, spurting out the wine in your grievous infancy.
sentences.n: πολλάκι is πολλάκις ‘often’. κατέδευσας is the aorist of καταδεύω ‘drench’, with χιτῶνα ‘tunic’ as its object and ἐπὶ στήθεσσι ‘on my chest’. οἴνου ἀποβλύζων is ‘spurting out wine’ (ἀποβλύζω ‘gush forth’). νηπιέῃ is ‘infancy’ (= νηπιείῃ), and ἀλεγεινῇ ‘grievous’ names the trouble of nursing a baby.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἐπὶ σοὶ μάλα πολλὰ πάθον καὶ πολλὰ μόγησα,
τὰ φρονέων ὅ μοι οὔ τι θεοὶ γόνον ἐξετέλειον
ἐξ ἐμεῦ·
sentences.i: So I suffered much for your sake and toiled much, reflecting that the gods were bringing no child of mine to birth;
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so, in this way’ looks back to the care of 485–491. ἐπὶ σοί is ‘for you’, and πάθον and μόγησα are aorists, both unaugmented (Attic ἔπαθον, ἐμόγησα). τὰ φρονέων is ‘thinking on these things’; ὅ (= ὅτι) ‘that’ introduces what he reflected. γόνον ἐξετέλειον is the imperfect of ἐκτελέω ‘bring to completion’: the gods were not completing the birth of any offspring from him. The next unit says what he did instead.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὲ παῖδα θεοῖς ἐπιείκελ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ
ποιεύμην, ἵνα μοί ποτ’ ἀεικέα λοιγὸν ἀμύνῃς.
sentences.l:
but you as a child, resembling the gods, Achilles,
I made my own, that you might some day ward off from me unseemly ruin.
sentences.i: but I made you my child, Achilles, like the gods, so that one day you might ward off unseemly ruin from me.
sentences.n: ποιεύμην is the imperfect middle of ποιέω in its epic form (= ἐποιούμην), and the middle voice means ‘made for myself’: σὲ παῖδα ποιεύμην is ‘I made you my child’, I adopted you. ἵνα … ἀμύνῃς is a purpose clause with the subjunctive. ἀεικέα λοιγόν ‘unseemly ruin’ is the phrase of 1.341 and 1.398; μοι with ἀμύνῃς is ‘from me, for me’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ Ἀχιλεῦ δάμασον θυμὸν μέγαν·
sentences.l: But, Achilles, subdue your great spirit;
sentences.i: But, Achilles, subdue your great spirit.
sentences.n: ἀλλά ‘but’ turns from the story of the past to the appeal. Ἀχιλεῦ is the vocative with a single λ, the edition’s spelling beside Ἀχιλλεῦ. δάμασον is the aorist imperative of δαμάζω ‘tame, subdue’, the verb for the breaking of horses. θυμός is ‘spirit’ here, not ‘heart’, since ἦτορ ‘heart’ follows in the next unit and the two words are kept apart.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τί σε χρὴ
νηλεὲς ἦτορ ἔχειν·
sentences.l:
and in no way is it needful for you
a pitiless heart to have;
sentences.i: and you must not keep a pitiless heart;
sentences.n: οὐδέ τι … χρή is ‘it is not at all necessary’, with the accusative σε and the infinitive ἔχειν. νηλεές ‘pitiless’ is the Odyssey’s rendering and qualifies ἦτορ ‘heart’, another word for the heart, close to θυμός but kept distinct.

sentences.t:
στρεπτοὶ δέ τε καὶ θεοὶ αὐτοί,
τῶν περ καὶ μείζων ἀρετὴ τιμή τε βίη τε.
sentences.l:
turnable are even the gods themselves,
whose excellence and honour and might are greater still.
sentences.i: Even the gods themselves can be turned, and theirs are greater excellence, honour and might.
sentences.n: στρεπτοί ‘turnable, able to be turned’ (from τρέπω) says that the gods can be moved from their purpose; δέ τε καί is ‘and also’, with τε marking a general truth. τῶν περ καί is ‘of whom, even so’, the relative ‘whose’, and μείζων ‘greater’ is singular, agreeing with the nearest noun ἀρετή and standing for all three. ἀρετή is ‘excellence’ (the Odyssey’s rendering), τιμή ‘honour’, and βίη ‘might’.

sentences.t:
καὶ μὲν τοὺς θυέεσσι καὶ εὐχωλῇς ἀγανῇσι
λοιβῇ τε κνίσῃ τε παρατρωπῶσ’ ἄνθρωποι
λισσόμενοι, ὅτε κέν τις ὑπερβήῃ καὶ ἁμάρτῃ.
sentences.l:
And indeed them with offerings and gentle prayers,
with libation and savour, men turn aside,
beseeching, whenever someone has transgressed and erred.
sentences.i: Even they are turned aside by men who beg them, with offerings and gentle prayers, with libation and the savour of sacrifice, whenever someone has transgressed and erred.
sentences.n: τοὺς is ‘them’, the gods of the last line, the article as a pronoun. παρατρωπῶσι is the contracted form of παρατρωπάω ‘turn aside, win over’, of the same family as στρεπτοί. θυέεσσι ‘offerings’ is the epic dative plural, εὐχωλῇς ἀγανῇσι ‘gentle prayers’ is the Odyssey’s phrase, and λοιβῇ ‘libation’ and κνίσῃ ‘savour’ (the smell of burnt fat) are as at 4.49. ὅτε κεν … ὑπερβήῃ καὶ ἁμάρτῃ is ‘whenever someone has overstepped and erred’, a general clause with subjunctives (ὑπερβαίνω ‘step over’, that is, transgress; ἁμαρτάνω ‘miss, err’).

sentences.t:
καὶ γάρ τε λιταί εἰσι Διὸς κοῦραι μεγάλοιο
χωλαί τε ῥυσαί τε παραβλῶπές τ’ ὀφθαλμώ,
αἵ ῥά τε καὶ μετόπισθ’ ἄτης ἀλέγουσι κιοῦσαι.
sentences.l:
For there are also Prayers, daughters of great Zeus,
lame and wrinkled and asquint in the two eyes,
who also take heed of Bewilderment, coming along behind her.
sentences.i: For there are also Prayers, daughters of great Zeus, lame and wrinkled and squinting with both eyes, who come on behind Bewilderment, taking heed of her.
sentences.n: καὶ γάρ τε ‘for indeed’ introduces an allegory by which Phoenix explains why a man should give way to prayer. λιταί, ‘Prayers’ (λιτή ‘prayer, entreaty’), are personified as daughters of Zeus, and ἄτη, ‘Bewilderment’ (the clouded state of mind that leads men to err, as at 9.115), is introduced in the next lines. χωλαί ‘lame’, ῥυσαί ‘wrinkled’ and παραβλῶπες ‘looking askance’ describe the Prayers’ appearance; ὀφθαλμώ is a dual accusative of respect, ‘in the two eyes’. ἄτης is the genitive after ἀλέγουσι ‘take heed of, care for’; μετόπισθε is the adverb ‘behind’, and κιοῦσαι is the participle of κίω ‘go’, ‘coming along’.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἄτη σθεναρή τε καὶ ἀρτίπος, οὕνεκα πάσας
πολλὸν ὑπεκπροθέει, φθάνει δέ τε πᾶσαν ἐπ’ αἶαν
βλάπτουσ’ ἀνθρώπους· αἳ δ’ ἐξακέονται ὀπίσσω.
sentences.l:
But Bewilderment is strong and sound of foot, so that all of them
far she outruns, and gets ahead over all the earth
harming men; and they heal afterwards.
sentences.i: But Bewilderment is strong and sound of foot, and so she outruns them all by far and gets ahead of them over the whole earth, harming men; and they, coming after, heal what she has done.
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ ἄτη: ἣ is ‘she’, the article as a pronoun, and ἄτη ‘Bewilderment’ is set against the Prayers. She is σθεναρή ‘strong’ and ἀρτίπος ‘sound of foot’ (ἄρτιος ‘fitting, sound’ + πούς); οὕνεκα is read ‘so that’, though it can also mean ‘because’. ὑπεκπροθέει is a long compound of θέω ‘run’, ‘runs out ahead of’, with πάσας ‘all of them’ (the Prayers), and φθάνει is ‘gets there first’. αἳ δ’ are the Prayers again; ἐξακέονται is a middle of ἀκέομαι ‘heal’, here ‘heal what has been done’, and ὀπίσσω ‘afterwards, behind’. The point is that the harm comes first and a prayer only heals it afterwards.

sentences.t:
ὃς μέν τ’ αἰδέσεται κούρας Διὸς ἆσσον ἰούσας,
τὸν δὲ μέγ’ ὤνησαν καί τ’ ἔκλυον εὐχομένοιο·
sentences.l:
Whoever shall revere the daughters of Zeus when they come near,
him greatly they benefit, and they hear him when he prays;
sentences.i: The man who reveres the daughters of Zeus when they draw near is greatly helped by them, and they hear him when he prays.
sentences.n: ὃς μέν τ’ … τὸν δέ sets up a general contrast, ‘whoever … him’. αἰδέσεται is the future of αἰδέομαι ‘revere’, with the force of a general condition, and ἆσσον ἰούσας is ‘coming nearer’ (ἆσσον is the comparative of ἄγχι). ὤνησαν (from ὀνίνημι ‘benefit’) and ἔκλυον are aorists in a general sense, ‘they benefit, they hear’, with τε marking a general truth. εὐχομένοιο is the genitive participle of εὔχομαι ‘pray’, after ἔκλυον. κούρας Διός ‘daughters of Zeus’ are the Prayers.

sentences.t:
ὃς δέ κ’ ἀνήνηται καί τε στερεῶς ἀποείπῃ,
λίσσονται δ’ ἄρα ταί γε Δία Κρονίωνα κιοῦσαι
τῷ ἄτην ἅμ’ ἕπεσθαι, ἵνα βλαφθεὶς ἀποτίσῃ.
sentences.l:
But whoever rejects them and sternly refuses,
they beseech, then, going to Zeus, the son of Cronus,
that Bewilderment go along with him, so that, harmed, he may pay.
sentences.i: But whoever rejects them and sternly refuses, they go to Zeus, the son of Cronus, and beg that Bewilderment go along with that man, so that, being harmed, he may pay for it.
sentences.n: ὃς δέ κ’ ἀνήνηται is the subjunctive of ἀναίνομαι ‘reject’ with κε, a general clause like the last, and ἀποείπῃ the subjunctive of ἀπεῖπον ‘refuse’ (as at 431), with the adverb στερεῶς ‘sternly, firmly’. λίσσονται … κιοῦσαι: the Prayers ‘beseech’ (the middle of λίσσομαι) Zeus, ‘going to’ him; ταί γε is the article as a pronoun, ‘they’, and Δία Κρονίωνα ‘Zeus, the son of Cronus’ is a fixed phrase. τῷ ἄτην ἅμ’ ἕπεσθαι is the content of the prayer: that Bewilderment ‘go along with’ (ἅμα + ἕπομαι) ‘him’ (τῷ, dative). ἵνα βλαφθεὶς ἀποτίσῃ is a purpose clause: βλαφθείς is the aorist passive participle of βλάπτω ‘harm’, and ἀποτίσῃ ‘pay (the price)’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ Ἀχιλεῦ πόρε καὶ σὺ Διὸς κούρῃσιν ἕπεσθαι
τιμήν, ἥ τ’ ἄλλων περ ἐπιγνάμπτει νόον ἐσθλῶν.
sentences.l:
But, Achilles, grant also you that honour follow the daughters of Zeus,
honour, which of others too bends the mind, good men’s.
sentences.i: But you too, Achilles, grant that honour attend the daughters of Zeus, the honour that bends the minds even of other good men.
sentences.n: πόρε is the aorist imperative of πορεῖν ‘grant, give’, followed by an infinitive, ‘grant that …’. τιμήν ‘honour’ is the accusative subject of ἕπεσθαι ‘follow, attend’, and Διὸς κούρῃσιν is the dative ‘the daughters of Zeus’, the Prayers: ‘grant that honour go with the Prayers’. ἥ τ’ … ἐπιγνάμπτει is the relative clause ‘which bends’ (ἐπιγνάμπτω ‘bend, turn’), with ἄλλων περ ἐσθλῶν ‘even of other good men’. νόον is the uncontracted νοῦν ‘mind’.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὲν γὰρ μὴ δῶρα φέροι τὰ δ’ ὄπισθ’ ὀνομάζοι
Ἀτρεΐδης, ἀλλ’ αἰὲν ἐπιζαφελῶς χαλεπαίνοι,
sentences.l:
For if he were not bringing gifts and naming the rest for later,
Atreus’-son, but were always furiously growing harsh,
sentences.i: For if the son of Atreus were not bringing gifts and naming the rest to follow later, but were forever furiously angry,
sentences.n: εἰ μὲν γάρ … is a supposition in the optative (φέροι, ὀνομάζοι, χαλεπαίνοι), put as the opposite of what is so; the main clause is in the next unit, and νῦν δέ at 519 states what is really so. τὰ δ’ ὄπισθ’ is ‘and those (gifts) for later’, and ὀνομάζω is ‘name, mention (as promised)’. Ἀτρεΐδης ‘the son of Atreus’ is Agamemnon. ἐπιζαφελῶς ‘furiously’ (the Odyssey’s rendering) goes with χαλεπαίνοι, from χαλεπός ‘harsh’.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἂν ἔγωγέ σε μῆνιν ἀπορρίψαντα κελοίμην
Ἀργείοισιν ἀμυνέμεναι χατέουσί περ ἔμπης·
sentences.l:
I would not myself urge you, having cast away your wrath,
to help the Argives, though they have need, all the same;
sentences.i: I would not urge you to cast off your wrath and help the Argives, in need though they are.
sentences.n: οὐκ ἂν … κελοίμην is ‘I would not urge’, the main clause of the supposition above (ἄν with the optative of κέλομαι). ἔγωγε is ‘I at least’; σε … ἀπορρίψαντα is ‘you, having thrown off’ (ἀπορρίπτω), and μῆνιν is ‘wrath’, the poem’s word for a lasting, god-sized anger. ἀμυνέμεναι is the epic infinitive (= ἀμύνειν) with the dative Ἀργείοισιν, ‘to help the Argives’; χατέουσι is ‘being in need’, with περ ἔμπης ‘even so, all the same’.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἅμα τ’ αὐτίκα πολλὰ διδοῖ τὰ δ’ ὄπισθεν ὑπέστη,
sentences.l: But now both at once many things he gives, and the later ones he has promised,
sentences.i: But as it is, he gives many gifts at once and has promised the rest for later,
sentences.n: νῦν δέ ‘but as it is’ states the facts against the supposition. διδοῖ is the epic form of δίδωσι ‘gives’. ἅμα τ’ αὐτίκα … τὰ δ’ ὄπισθεν pairs the gifts given at once with those promised for later; ὑπέστη is the aorist of ὑφίσταμαι ‘undertake, promise’, as at 445 (ὑποσταίη).

sentences.t:
ἄνδρας δὲ λίσσεσθαι ἐπιπροέηκεν ἀρίστους
κρινάμενος κατὰ λαὸν Ἀχαιϊκόν, οἵ τε σοὶ αὐτῷ
φίλτατοι Ἀργείων·
sentences.i: and he has sent men to beg you, the best, picked out from the Achaean army, who are dearest to you yourself of the Argives.
sentences.n: λίσσεσθαι ‘to beseech’ is an infinitive of purpose, with σέ understood; ἐπιπροέηκεν is the aorist of ἐπιπροΐημι ‘send forth to’, with Agamemnon as its subject. κρινάμενος ‘having picked out’ (κρίνω in the middle, ‘choose for oneself’). κατὰ λαὸν Ἀχαιϊκόν is ‘from the Achaean army’, and οἵ τε σοὶ αὐτῷ φίλτατοι Ἀργείων is ‘who are dearest to you yourself of the Argives’, the envoys now in Achilles’ hut, Phoenix himself among them.

sentences.t:
τῶν μὴ σύ γε μῦθον ἐλέγξῃς
μηδὲ πόδας·
sentences.l:
Of these do not you put to shame the word
nor the feet;
sentences.i: Do not you bring shame on their words, or on their coming;
sentences.n: τῶν is ‘of them’, the envoys, a genitive of possession with both μῦθον and πόδας, ‘their word, their feet’. ἐλέγξῃς is the aorist subjunctive of ἐλέγχω in a prohibition (μὴ σύ γε … ἐλέγξῃς): ‘put to shame, disgrace’. πόδας ‘feet’ stands for their journey on foot, their coming. The negative continues with μηδέ ‘nor’.

sentences.t: πρὶν δ’ οὔ τι νεμεσσητὸν κεχολῶσθαι.
sentences.l: but before this it was not at all a thing to resent, to be angry.
sentences.i: Until now there was no reason to resent your being angry.
sentences.n: πρίν here is the adverb ‘before, until now’, set against the gifts that are offered now. νεμεσσητόν is a verbal adjective from νεμεσάω, ‘a thing to resent’; οὔ τι νεμεσσητὸν κεχολῶσθαι has no verb, ‘(it was) not at all a thing to resent, to be angry’. κεχολῶσθαι is the perfect passive infinitive of χολόω, ‘to be angry’.

sentences.t:
οὕτω καὶ τῶν πρόσθεν ἐπευθόμεθα κλέα ἀνδρῶν
ἡρώων, ὅτε κέν τιν’ ἐπιζάφελος χόλος ἵκοι·
sentences.l:
So also of the men of before we have learned the glories,
of heroes, whenever violent anger came upon any:
sentences.i: So, too, we have learned the glories of the heroes of old, whenever furious anger came upon any of them:
sentences.n: οὕτω ‘so, in this way’ leads from Phoenix’s argument to the precedent. τῶν πρόσθεν ‘of those before’ goes with κλέα ἀνδρῶν ἡρώων ‘the glories of men, heroes’ (κλέα the plural of κλέος, as in the Odyssey’s ‘the glories of men’). ἐπευθόμεθα, from πεύθομαι (the epic form of πυνθάνομαι), is a past tense, ‘we learned by inquiry’: the Achaeans know these heroes only from song. ὅτε κέν … ἵκοι is a general condition in the past, with the optative: ‘whenever violent anger came on someone’. ἐπιζάφελος is a rare word, ‘violent, furious’, the adjective of ἐπιζαφελῶς above.

sentences.t: δωρητοί τε πέλοντο παράρρητοί τ’ ἐπέεσσι.
sentences.l: They were to be won by gifts and to be talked round with words.
sentences.i: They could be won by gifts and talked round with words.
sentences.n: δωρητοί and παράρρητοι are verbal adjectives: ‘to be won by gifts’ (δῶρον) and ‘to be talked round’ (παρά + the root of εἰπεῖν ‘speak’). πέλοντο is ‘were’, and ἐπέεσσι is the epic dative plural, ‘with words’. The precedent: angry heroes of old could be appeased by gifts and persuasion.

sentences.t:
μέμνημαι τόδε ἔργον ἐγὼ πάλαι οὔ τι νέον γε
ὡς ἦν·
sentences.l:
I remember this deed, I, from long ago, not at all new,
how it was;
sentences.i: I myself remember this deed of long ago, no new one, how it was;
sentences.n: μέμνημαι is the perfect used as a present, ‘I remember’, with the accusative ἔργον ‘deed’, here a story. πάλαι οὔ τι νέον γε is ‘long ago, not at all new’, and ὡς ἦν ‘how it was’ is an indirect question after μέμνημαι. The ano teleia leads into the statement of the next unit.

sentences.t: ἐν δ’ ὑμῖν ἐρέω πάντεσσι φίλοισι.
sentences.l: and among you I shall tell it, all of you friends.
sentences.i: and I will tell it among you, all of you my friends.
sentences.n: ἐρέω is the future of λέγω, ‘I shall tell’. ἐν ὑμῖν πάντεσσι φίλοισι is ‘among you all, friends’ (πάντεσσι the epic dative plural): the hearers are Achilles and the other envoys.

sentences.t:
Κουρῆτές τ’ ἐμάχοντο καὶ Αἰτωλοὶ μενεχάρμαι
ἀμφὶ πόλιν Καλυδῶνα καὶ ἀλλήλους ἐνάριζον,
sentences.l:
The Curetes fought and the Aetolians, steadfast in the fray,
around the city of Calydon, and one another they slew,
sentences.i: The Curetes and the Aetolians, steadfast in the fray, were fighting around the city of Calydon and killing one another,
sentences.n: A new story begins, told as a precedent: the Curetes and the Aetolians fight over Calydon, the Aetolians’ city. μενεχάρμαι (from μένω ‘stand fast’ and χάρμη ‘fight’) is a stock epithet of fighters, ‘steadfast in the fray’. ἐνάριζον is the imperfect of ἐναρίζω ‘kill’ (properly, to strip a slain man of his armour). The imperfects ἐμάχοντο and ἐνάριζον describe a war that goes on.

sentences.t:
Αἰτωλοὶ μὲν ἀμυνόμενοι Καλυδῶνος ἐραννῆς,
Κουρῆτες δὲ διαπραθέειν μεμαῶτες Ἄρηϊ.
sentences.l:
the Aetolians defending delightful Calydon,
and the Curetes eager to sack it utterly in war.
sentences.i: the Aetolians defending delightful Calydon, and the Curetes eager to sack it in war.
sentences.n: ἀμυνόμενοι is the middle participle of ἀμύνω, ‘defending themselves, fighting in defence’, with the genitive Καλυδῶνος ‘for Calydon’. ἐραννῆς ‘delightful’ is the Odyssey’s rendering. διαπραθέειν is the aorist infinitive of διαπέρθω ‘sack utterly’, after μεμαῶτες ‘eager’ (the perfect participle of μέμονα); Ἄρηϊ is the dative of Ares, standing for war: ‘in war’.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ τοῖσι κακὸν χρυσόθρονος Ἄρτεμις ὦρσε
χωσαμένη ὅ οἱ οὔ τι θαλύσια γουνῷ ἀλωῆς
Οἰνεὺς ῥέξ’·
sentences.i: For on them, too, golden-throned Artemis roused up an evil, angered because Oeneus had not offered her first-fruits on the rich ground of his orchard;
sentences.n: καὶ γάρ ‘for indeed’ explains how the war came about: Artemis roused an evil ‘for them’ (τοῖσι, the Aetolians) because Oeneus, king of Calydon, left her out of his offerings. χρυσόθρονος ‘golden-throned’ is an epithet she shares with Hera, and ὦρσε is the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’. χωσαμένη is the aorist participle of χώομαι ‘be incensed’; ὅ is ‘because’ (= ὅτι) and οἱ ‘to her’. θαλύσια are offerings of the first produce of the harvest, and γουνῷ ἀλωῆς is ‘on the rich ground of the orchard’, though the exact sense of γουνός (rising ground, or a fertile plot) is not certain. ῥέξ’ is the unaugmented aorist ῥέξε of ῥέζω ‘do, offer’; 536 has the augmented ἔρρεξε.

sentences.t:
ἄλλοι δὲ θεοὶ δαίνυνθ’ ἑκατόμβας,
οἴῃ δ’ οὐκ ἔρρεξε Διὸς κούρῃ μεγάλοιο.
sentences.l:
but the other gods feasted on hecatombs,
and to her alone he did not sacrifice, the daughter of great Zeus.
sentences.i: The other gods feasted on his hecatombs, but to her alone, the daughter of great Zeus, he made no offering.
sentences.n: ἄλλοι θεοί ‘the other gods’ are the subject of δαίνυνθ’ (= δαίνυντο, ‘feasted’), with ἑκατόμβας ‘hecatombs’ as the object: they received Oeneus’ sacrifices. A hecatomb is properly a sacrifice of a hundred oxen. οἴῃ is the dative ‘to her alone’, agreeing with κούρῃ Διὸς μεγάλοιο ‘the daughter of great Zeus’, so Artemis is named by her father. ἔρρεξε is the augmented aorist of ῥέζω, repeating the verb of 535.

sentences.t: ἢ λάθετ’ ἢ οὐκ ἐνόησεν·
sentences.l: Either he forgot, or he did not think of it;
sentences.i: Either he forgot, or he never thought of it.
sentences.n: λάθετ’ is the aorist middle λάθετο of λήθομαι ‘forget’, and ἐνόησεν the aorist of νοέω ‘notice, think of’; ἢ … ἢ is ‘either … or’. Phoenix gives two possible explanations of the neglect and does not choose between them.

sentences.t: ἀάσατο δὲ μέγα θυμῷ.
sentences.l: and he was greatly bewildered in his heart.
sentences.i: and he was greatly bewildered in his heart.
sentences.n: ἀάσατο is the aorist middle of ἀάω, ‘cloud the mind, bewilder’; the noun of the same family is ἄτη (‘Bewilderment’), which Phoenix has just made a person (505–512), so the king’s neglect is itself an act of ἄτη. μέγα is adverbial, ‘greatly’, and θυμῷ is ‘in his heart’.

sentences.t:
ἣ δὲ χολωσαμένη δῖον γένος ἰοχέαιρα
ὦρσεν ἔπι χλούνην σῦν ἄγριον ἀργιόδοντα,
ὃς κακὰ πόλλ’ ἕρδεσκεν ἔθων Οἰνῆος ἀλωήν·
sentences.i: And she, who showers her arrows, angered at the heavenly race, roused against them a lone, wild, white-toothed boar, which was always doing great harm, haunting the orchard of Oeneus;
sentences.n: ἰοχέαιρα, ‘the arrow-pourer’, is Artemis; the house rendering of the epithet is ‘who showers her arrows’. δῖον γένος is most naturally the accusative object of her anger, ‘the heavenly race’, that is, Oeneus’ line; the neuter ending speaks against taking it as an epithet of the goddess. ὦρσεν ἔπι is a tmesis, ‘roused against’. The meaning of χλούνην is not known, the ancient guesses being ‘solitary’ and others, and ‘lone’ is only a guess; σῦν ἄγριον ‘wild boar’ and ἀργιόδοντα ‘white-toothed’ (the Odyssey’s rendering) are plain. ἕρδεσκεν is an iterative imperfect, ‘used to do’, and ἔθων is probably the participle of ἔθω ‘be accustomed’, so ‘haunting’ is the traditional sense and not a certain one.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δ’ ὅ γε προθέλυμνα χαμαὶ βάλε δένδρεα μακρὰ
αὐτῇσιν ῥίζῃσι καὶ αὐτοῖς ἄνθεσι μήλων.
sentences.l:
and many tall trees he threw to the ground, torn up from the base,
with the very roots and with the very blossoms of the apples.
sentences.i: He threw many tall trees to the ground, torn up from the base, roots and all, with the very blossoms of their apples.
sentences.n: ὅ γε is ‘he’, the boar. προθέλυμνα is an adjective used as an adverb, ‘from the foundation’, so ‘torn up from the base’; θέλυμνα are the roots or the base of a tree. βάλε is the unaugmented aorist of βάλλω, ‘threw down’. αὐτῇσιν ῥίζῃσι ‘with the roots themselves’ and αὐτοῖς ἄνθεσι ‘with the very blossoms’ stress that nothing was left standing. μήλων is here the genitive plural of μῆλον ‘apple, fruit’, not of μῆλα ‘flocks’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ υἱὸς Οἰνῆος ἀπέκτεινεν Μελέαγρος
πολλέων ἐκ πολίων θηρήτορας ἄνδρας ἀγείρας
καὶ κύνας·
sentences.i: But the son of Oeneus, Meleager, killed it, having gathered hunters from many cities, and dogs.
sentences.n: τόν is ‘him’, the boar, the article as a pronoun. Meleager, son of Oeneus, kills it; ἀπέκτεινεν is the aorist of ἀποκτείνω ‘kill’. πολλέων ἐκ πολίων has the epic genitive plural πολλέων (= πολλῶν), ‘from many cities’; θηρήτορας ἄνδρας is ‘hunter men’ (ἄνδρας added in apposition to the noun θηρήτορας ‘hunters’); ἀγείρας is the aorist participle of ἀγείρω ‘gather’, with ἄνδρας and κύνας ‘dogs’ as its objects.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν γάρ κε δάμη παύροισι βροτοῖσι·
sentences.l: for not by few mortals could he have been subdued;
sentences.i: for he could not have been overcome by a few mortals.
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ ‘for truly not’ explains why so many were gathered. δάμη is the aorist passive of δαμάζω ‘subdue’ (the verb of 496), and with κε it means ‘could not have been subdued’. παύροισι βροτοῖσι is ‘few mortals’. The ano teleia leads into the statement of the boar’s size.

sentences.t: τόσσος ἔην, πολλοὺς δὲ πυρῆς ἐπέβησ’ ἀλεγεινῆς.
sentences.l: so great he was, and many he set upon the grievous pyre.
sentences.i: Such was his size, and he put many on the grievous pyre.
sentences.n: τόσσος ἔην is ‘so great he was’ (ἔην = ἦν). ἐπέβησ’ is the aorist of ἐπιβαίνω in its causative use, ‘made to mount’, so ‘set upon’ the pyre: the boar killed many men, and they were burned. ἀλεγεινῆς ‘grievous’ (the Odyssey’s rendering) agrees with πυρῆς.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἀμφ’ αὐτῷ θῆκε πολὺν κέλαδον καὶ ἀϋτὴν
ἀμφὶ συὸς κεφαλῇ καὶ δέρματι λαχνήεντι,
Κουρήτων τε μεσηγὺ καὶ Αἰτωλῶν μεγαθύμων.
sentences.l:
And she around it made much din and battle-cry,
about the boar’s head and its hairy hide,
between the Curetes and the great-hearted Aetolians.
sentences.i: And she made a great din and battle-cry around it, over the boar’s head and its hairy hide, between the Curetes and the great-hearted Aetolians.
sentences.n: ἣ is ‘she’, Artemis, still the subject: having sent the boar, she now sets the two peoples fighting over its carcass. ἀμφ’ αὐτῷ is ‘around it’, the dead boar. κέλαδον ‘din’ and ἀϋτήν ‘battle-cry’ are the sounds of the fighting; the prize is συὸς κεφαλῇ καὶ δέρματι λαχνήεντι, ‘the boar’s head and its hairy hide’ (datives after ἀμφί, ‘over’). μεσηγύ ‘between’ takes the genitives Κουρήτων … Αἰτωλῶν, and μεγαθύμων ‘great-hearted’ is a stock epithet.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα μὲν οὖν Μελέαγρος ἄρηι φίλος πολέμιζε,
τόφρα δὲ Κουρήτεσσι κακῶς ἦν, οὐδὲ δύναντο
τείχεος ἔκτοσθεν μίμνειν πολέες περ ἐόντες·
sentences.i: Now as long as Meleager, dear to Ares, kept fighting, it went badly for the Curetes, and they could not hold their ground outside the wall, many as they were;
sentences.n: ὄφρα … τόφρα pairs ‘as long as … for that time’. ἄρηι φίλος is ‘dear to Ares’: ἄρηι is the dative of Ἄρης, printed with a small initial letter in the edition, and φίλος has the passive sense ‘dear’ (as in ἀρηΐφιλος). κακῶς ἦν with the dative Κουρήτεσσι is ‘it was ill for the Curetes’. τείχεος ἔκτοσθεν is ‘outside the wall’ (τείχεος the epic genitive of τεῖχος), μίμνειν ‘to stay, hold out’, and πολέες περ ἐόντες ‘though they were many’ (πολέες = πολλοί).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ Μελέαγρον ἔδυ χόλος, ὅς τε καὶ ἄλλων
οἰδάνει ἐν στήθεσσι νόον πύκα περ φρονεόντων,
sentences.l:
But when anger entered Meleager, which swells too of others
in their chests the mind, though they think shrewdly,
sentences.i: But when anger entered Meleager, the anger that swells the mind in the breast even of others who are shrewd of thought,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή marks the turning-point: ‘but when’. ἔδυ is the aorist of δύω ‘enter’, here with the accusative Μελέαγρον as the one entered, and χόλος is ‘anger’. The relative clause ὅς τε … οἰδάνει ‘which swells’ (οἰδάνω ‘make swell’) is a general statement, with τε; ἄλλων … φρονεόντων is ‘of others, even though they think shrewdly’ (φρονεόντων is the uncontracted participle of φρονέω, and πύκα ‘closely, shrewdly’). νόον is ‘mind’, and ἐν στήθεσσι ‘in the chest’.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ὃ μητρὶ φίλῃ Ἀλθαίῃ χωόμενος κῆρ
κεῖτο παρὰ μνηστῇ ἀλόχῳ καλῇ Κλεοπάτρῃ
κούρῃ Μαρπήσσης καλλισφύρου Εὐηνίνης
Ἴδεώ θ’, ὃς κάρτιστος ἐπιχθονίων γένετ’ ἀνδρῶν
τῶν τότε·
sentences.l:
he, indeed, with his dear mother Althaea incensed in heart
lay beside his wedded wife, fair Cleopatra,
the daughter of Marpessa, fair-ankled, Evenus’ daughter,
and of Idas, who was the strongest of men upon the earth
of those days;
sentences.i: he, incensed at heart with his dear mother Althaea, lay beside his wedded wife, fair Cleopatra, the daughter of fair-ankled Marpessa, Evenus’ daughter, and of Idas, who was the strongest of the men then living on earth;
sentences.n: ἤτοι ὃ resumes the subject, Meleager, after the general remark; ὃ is the article as a pronoun. χωόμενος κῆρ is ‘incensed in heart’ (κῆρ is an accusative of respect), with the dative μητρὶ φίλῃ Ἀλθαίῃ ‘with his dear mother Althaea’, the source of his anger. κεῖτο is ‘lay’, with παρά and the dative, ‘beside’; μνηστῇ ἀλόχῳ is ‘wedded wife’ (μνηστός ‘wooed’, that is, lawfully married), and καλῇ ‘fair’. Meleager’s withdrawal into anger, like Achilles’, is a retreat to his own chamber. The sentence runs on through 557–559: κούρῃ Μαρπήσσης καλλισφύρου Εὐηνίνης is ‘the daughter of fair-ankled Marpessa, Evenus’ daughter’, in apposition with Κλεοπάτρῃ, and Ἴδεώ θ’ (= Ἴδεώ τε) adds ‘and of Idas’, her father, called κάρτιστος ‘strongest’ of ἐπιχθονίων ἀνδρῶν ‘men upon the earth’, τῶν τότε ‘of those of that time’; the source prints no stop at the end of 556, so the two stretches are one unit. The next lines say why Idas is brought in.

sentences.t:
καί ῥα ἄνακτος ἐναντίον εἵλετο τόξον
Φοίβου Ἀπόλλωνος καλλισφύρου εἵνεκα νύμφης,
sentences.l:
and he, indeed, against the lord took up a bow,
Phoebus Apollo, for the sake of the fair-ankled bride;
sentences.i: and he it was who took up the bow against the lord, Phoebus Apollo, for the sake of his fair-ankled bride;
sentences.n: καί ῥα continues the description of Idas: ‘and he indeed …’. ἄνακτος … Φοίβου Ἀπόλλωνος is ‘the lord, Phoebus Apollo’, in the genitive after ἐναντίον ‘facing, against’. εἵλετο is the aorist middle of αἱρέω ‘take up’. εἵνεκα ‘for the sake of’ governs νύμφης, a young woman, here the bride Marpessa, called καλλισφύρου ‘fair-ankled’ again.

sentences.t:
τὴν δὲ τότ’ ἐν μεγάροισι πατὴρ καὶ πότνια μήτηρ
Ἀλκυόνην καλέεσκον ἐπώνυμον, οὕνεκ’ ἄρ’ αὐτῆς
μήτηρ ἀλκυόνος πολυπενθέος οἶτον ἔχουσα
κλαῖεν ὅ μιν ἑκάεργος ἀνήρπασε Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.l:
And her then in the halls her father and lady mother
Alcyone used to call, as a by-name, because her own
mother, having the fate of the much-grieving halcyon,
wept that far-working Phoebus Apollo had snatched her away;
sentences.i: In the halls her father and lady mother then used to call her Alcyone, as a surname, because her mother, having the fate of the much-grieving halcyon, wept that Phoebus Apollo, who works from afar, had snatched her away;
sentences.n: τὴν is Cleopatra again. Her parents called her Ἀλκυόνη ‘Alcyone’ ἐπώνυμον, ‘as a by-name’, after her mother’s grief: the mother was οἶτον ἔχουσα ‘having the lot’ of the ἀλκυών, the halcyon or kingfisher, a bird whose cry was heard as mourning. καλέεσκον is an iterative imperfect, ‘used to call’, and κλαῖεν the unaugmented imperfect of κλαίω ‘weep’. ὅ is ‘because’ (= ὅτι), and μιν ‘her’ is most naturally the mother herself, whom Apollo snatched away (ἀνήρπασε, from ἀναρπάζω). πότνια μήτηρ is ‘lady mother’, and ἑκάεργος is ‘who works from afar’, an epithet of disputed sense.

sentences.t:
τῇ ὅ γε παρκατέλεκτο χόλον θυμαλγέα πέσσων
ἐξ ἀρέων μητρὸς κεχολωμένος, ἥ ῥα θεοῖσι
πόλλ’ ἀχέουσ’ ἠρᾶτο κασιγνήτοιο φόνοιο,
sentences.l:
Beside her he lay, brooding heart-paining anger,
angered by the curses of his mother, who, to the gods
much grieving, had prayed over the slaying of her brother,
sentences.i: Beside her he lay, brooding his heart-paining anger, angered by his mother’s curses, she who, grieving greatly, had prayed to the gods over the killing of her brother,
sentences.n: τῇ is ‘beside her’ (Cleopatra) and ὅ γε ‘he’; παρκατέλεκτο is the aorist of παρακατάλεγομαι ‘lie down beside’. χόλον θυμαλγέα πέσσων: πέσσω is ‘cook, digest’, here ‘brood over’, and θυμαλγέα is ‘heart-paining’ (θυμός + ἄλγος). ἐξ ἀρέων … κεχολωμένος: ἀρέων is the genitive plural of ἀρά ‘prayer, curse’, so the mother’s curses are the cause of the anger. The relative ἥ ῥα … ἠρᾶτο ‘who had prayed’ (ἀράομαι) takes the genitive κασιγνήτοιο φόνοιο ‘over the killing of her brother’ (the singular ‘brother’ is as printed); the killer is not named in these lines. ἀχέουσα is ‘grieving’.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δὲ καὶ γαῖαν πολυφόρβην χερσὶν ἀλοία
κικλήσκουσ’ Ἀΐδην καὶ ἐπαινὴν Περσεφόνειαν
πρόχνυ καθεζομένη, δεύοντο δὲ δάκρυσι κόλποι,
παιδὶ δόμεν θάνατον·
sentences.l:
and often too the much-nourishing earth with her hands she beat,
calling on Hades and grim Persephone,
kneeling forward, and with tears her lap was wet,
to give death to her child;
sentences.i: and many times she beat the much-nourishing earth with her hands, calling on Hades and grim Persephone, kneeling forward while her lap was wet with tears, to give her child death;
sentences.n: πολλά is adverbial, ‘many times’, with ἀλοία, the imperfect of ἀλοιάω ‘strike, beat’; striking the earth was a gesture to call the powers below. The earth is γαῖαν πολυφόρβην ‘much-nourishing’ (πολύς + φορβή ‘food’). κικλήσκουσα (= καλοῦσα) ‘calling on’ takes Ἀΐδην ‘Hades’ and ἐπαινὴν Περσεφόνειαν ‘grim Persephone’ (the epithet of 457). πρόχνυ καθεζομένη is ‘sitting bent forward on her knees’, and κόλποι, the folds of her dress at the breast, are ‘her lap’, wet with tears. παιδὶ δόμεν θάνατον is an infinitive of the request, ‘(praying) to give death to her child’ (δόμεν = δοῦναι).

sentences.t:
τῆς δ’ ἠεροφοῖτις Ἐρινὺς
ἔκλυεν ἐξ Ἐρέβεσφιν ἀμείλιχον ἦτορ ἔχουσα.
sentences.l:
And her the mist-walking Erinys
heard, from Erebus, having an ungentle heart.
sentences.i: The Erinys who walks in the mist heard her from Erebus, with an unrelenting heart.
sentences.n: τῆς is the genitive after ἔκλυεν ‘heard’, of the person heard: ‘her’, Althaea. ἠεροφοῖτις is ‘walking in the mist’ (ἠέρι ‘mist’ + φοιτάω ‘go to and fro’), an epithet of the Erinys. ἐξ Ἐρέβεσφιν: the ending -φιν is an old case ending, here ‘from Erebus’, the darkness under the earth. ἀμείλιχον ἦτορ ἔχουσα is ‘having an unrelenting heart’; ἀμείλιχος is ‘ungentle’ (ἀ- + the root of μειλίσσω ‘soothe’). The Erinys, like the gods of 454–457, answers a curse.

sentences.t:
τῶν δὲ τάχ’ ἀμφὶ πύλας ὅμαδος καὶ δοῦπος ὀρώρει
πύργων βαλλομένων·
sentences.l:
And of them soon around the gates the din and thud had arisen,
of towers being struck;
sentences.i: Soon, around their gates, the uproar and the thud of towers under attack arose;
sentences.n: τῶν is ‘their’, the besieged Aetolians’, and τάχα is ‘soon’. ὅμαδος ‘din, noise of a crowd’ and δοῦπος ‘thud, crash’ are the sounds of the assault; ὀρώρει is the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι, ‘had arisen’, used like an imperfect; πύργων βαλλομένων is a genitive depending on ὅμαδος and δοῦπος, ‘of towers being struck’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ λίσσοντο γέροντες
Αἰτωλῶν, πέμπον δὲ θεῶν ἱερῆας ἀρίστους,
ἐξελθεῖν καὶ ἀμῦναι ὑποσχόμενοι μέγα δῶρον·
sentences.i: and the elders of the Aetolians begged him, and sent the best priests of the gods, to come out and help, promising a great gift;
sentences.n: τόν is ‘him’, Meleager. The γέροντες Αἰτωλῶν ‘elders of the Aetolians’ and the priests, θεῶν ἱερῆας ἀρίστους ‘the best priests of the gods’, come to him as envoys, as Phoenix and the others have come to Achilles. ἐξελθεῖν καὶ ἀμῦναι ‘to come out and help’ are aorist infinitives of the request after λίσσοντο, and ὑποσχόμενοι ‘promising’ is from ὑπισχνέομαι. The gift is described in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὁππόθι πιότατον πεδίον Καλυδῶνος ἐραννῆς,
ἔνθά μιν ἤνωγον τέμενος περικαλλὲς ἑλέσθαι
πεντηκοντόγυον, τὸ μὲν ἥμισυ οἰνοπέδοιο,
ἥμισυ δὲ ψιλὴν ἄροσιν πεδίοιο ταμέσθαι.
sentences.l:
where the plain of delightful Calydon is richest,
there they bade him choose a very fair precinct
of fifty gyes, half of it vine-land,
and half bare ploughland of the plain to cut out.
sentences.i: Where the plain of delightful Calydon was richest, there they bade him choose a very fair estate of fifty acres, half of it vineyard land, and half bare ploughland to be cut out of the plain.
sentences.n: ὁππόθι … ἔνθα is ‘where … there’: the best land of the plain is offered. πιότατον is the superlative of πίων ‘rich, fat’. ἤνωγον is the imperfect of ἄνωγα ‘bid’, with μιν ‘him’ and the infinitives ἑλέσθαι ‘to choose’ and ταμέσθαι ‘to cut out for himself’. τέμενος ‘precinct’ is a plot of land set apart, and περικαλλές is ‘very fair’ (περι- ‘very’). πεντηκοντόγυον is ‘of fifty γύαι’: a γύης is a measure of land whose size is not known, and ‘acres’ is only a rough equivalent. τὸ μὲν ἥμισυ … ἥμισυ δέ is ‘half … and half’; οἰνοπέδοιο ‘vineyard land’; ψιλήν ‘bare’, without trees; ἄροσιν ‘ploughland’; and πεδίοιο ‘of the plain’ is the land from which it is cut.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δέ μιν λιτάνευε γέρων ἱππηλάτα Οἰνεὺς
οὐδοῦ ἐπεμβεβαὼς ὑψηρεφέος θαλάμοιο
σείων κολλητὰς σανίδας γουνούμενος υἱόν·
sentences.i: And many times Oeneus, the old horse-driver, entreated him, standing on the threshold of the high-roofed chamber, shaking the close-joined doors, beseeching his son;
sentences.n: πολλά is ‘many times’. λιτάνευε is the imperfect of λιτανεύω ‘entreat’, and the subject is γέρων ἱππηλάτα Οἰνεύς, the same stock pair as for Peleus and Nestor. οὐδοῦ ἐπεμβεβαώς is the perfect participle of ἐπεμβαίνω ‘stand upon’, with the genitive of the threshold; ὑψηρεφέος θαλάμοιο is ‘of the high-roofed chamber’. σείων ‘shaking’ the κολλητὰς σανίδας ‘close-joined doors’ (σανίδες are boards; κολλητός is ‘glued’, that is, fitted tight) shows the father at the door of his son’s room. γουνούμενος, from γουνόομαι ‘beseech’, comes from γόνυ ‘knee’ but does not say that the knees are clasped.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δὲ τόν γε κασίγνηται καὶ πότνια μήτηρ
ἐλλίσσονθ’·
sentences.l:
And many times him his sisters and lady mother
besought;
sentences.i: Many times, too, his sisters and his lady mother begged him;
sentences.n: κασίγνηται ‘sisters’ and πότνια μήτηρ ‘lady mother’ are the subjects of ἐλλίσσοντο, the imperfect of ἐλλίσσομαι ‘beseech’ (elided ἐλλίσσονθ’). τόν γε is ‘him’, Meleager. The mother who prayed against him above is among those who now beg.

sentences.t: ὃ δὲ μᾶλλον ἀναίνετο·
sentences.l: but he rejected them the more;
sentences.i: but he rejected them all the more.
sentences.n: ὃ δέ is ‘but he’; μᾶλλον ‘the more’; ἀναίνετο is the imperfect of ἀναίνομαι ‘reject’, the verb of 510.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δ’ ἑταῖροι,
οἵ οἱ κεδνότατοι καὶ φίλτατοι ἦσαν ἁπάντων·
sentences.l:
and many times his companions,
who were most trusty and dearest to him of all;
sentences.i: and his companions begged him many times over, the most trusty and the dearest to him of all;
sentences.n: The verb is understood from ἐλλίσσοντο above: ‘and (they besought him) many times, his companions’. ἑταῖροι are ‘companions’; οἵ is the relative ‘who’ and οἱ the dative ‘to him’. κεδνότατοι is the superlative of κεδνός ‘trusty’, with φίλτατοι ‘dearest’ (the superlative of φίλος) and ἁπάντων ‘of all’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὧς τοῦ θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἔπειθον,
πρίν γ’ ὅτε δὴ θάλαμος πύκ’ ἐβάλλετο, τοὶ δ’ ἐπὶ πύργων
βαῖνον Κουρῆτες καὶ ἐνέπρηθον μέγα ἄστυ.
sentences.l:
But not even so his heart in his chest did they persuade,
until indeed the chamber was thickly struck, and upon the towers
were climbing the Curetes and were burning the great town.
sentences.i: But not even so could they move the heart in his chest, until his chamber was being thickly pelted and the Curetes were climbing the towers and setting fire to the great town.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὧς is ‘but not even so’; τοῦ is the pronoun ‘his’, and ἔπειθον is the imperfect of πείθω ‘persuade’, ‘kept trying to persuade and could not’. πρίν γ’ ὅτε δή is ‘until the time when’, as at 488. θάλαμος πύκ’ ἐβάλλετο is ‘the chamber was thickly struck’ (πύκα ‘thickly, in quick succession’), as missiles fell on it. τοὶ δ’ are the Curetes (the article as a pronoun), who were climbing ἐπὶ πύργων ‘upon the towers’. ἐνέπρηθον is the imperfect of ἐμπρήθω ‘set on fire’, and μέγα ἄστυ is ‘the great town’ (the Odyssey’s ἄστυ ‘town’).

sentences.t:
καὶ τότε δὴ Μελέαγρον ἐΰζωνος παράκοιτις
λίσσετ’ ὀδυρομένη, καί οἱ κατέλεξεν ἅπαντα
κήδε’, ὅσ’ ἀνθρώποισι πέλει τῶν ἄστυ ἁλώῃ·
sentences.l:
And then indeed Meleager his well-girdled consort
besought, lamenting, and told over to him all
the sorrows that come to men whose town is taken:
sentences.i: And then, at last, his well-girdled wife begged Meleager, weeping, and told over to him all the sorrows that befall men whose town is taken;
sentences.n: Μελέαγρον is the object of λίσσετ’ (λίσσετο, the imperfect of λίσσομαι ‘beseech’), and the subject, ἐΰζωνος παράκοιτις ‘well-girdled consort’, is Cleopatra, named at 556. ὀδυρομένη is ‘lamenting’, and κατέλεξεν the aorist of καταλέγω ‘recount, enumerate’. κήδεα (κήδε’) are ‘sorrows’, with ὅσα ‘all that’; ἀνθρώποισι … τῶν ἄστυ ἁλώῃ is ‘to men whose town is taken’ (ἁλώῃ the aorist subjunctive of ἁλίσκομαι).

sentences.t:
ἄνδρας μὲν κτείνουσι, πόλιν δέ τε πῦρ ἀμαθύνει,
τέκνα δέ τ’ ἄλλοι ἄγουσι βαθυζώνους τε γυναῖκας.
sentences.l:
Men they kill, and the city fire levels to dust,
and children others lead away, and deep-girdled women.
sentences.i: They kill the men, fire reduces the city to dust, and others lead away the children and the deep-girdled women.
sentences.n: The sorrows are listed as a general truth (the τε marks it). κτείνουσι ‘they kill’ has no stated subject, ‘the enemy’; ἀμαθύνει ‘reduces to dust’ (from ἄμαθος ‘sand, dust’) has πῦρ ‘fire’ as its subject; ἄλλοι ‘others’ ἄγουσι ‘lead away’ the captives. βαθυζώνους ‘deep-girdled’ describes the women (βαθύς ‘deep’ + ζώνη ‘girdle’) as a stock epithet, and the exact picture it draws is not certain.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ὠρίνετο θυμὸς ἀκούοντος κακὰ ἔργα,
βῆ δ’ ἰέναι, χροῒ δ’ ἔντε’ ἐδύσετο παμφανόωντα.
sentences.l:
And his heart was stirred as he heard the evil deeds,
and he set out to go, and on his skin the gear he put, all-shining.
sentences.i: His heart was stirred as he heard of these evil deeds, and he set out to go, and put the all-shining gear on his body.
sentences.n: τοῦ … θυμός is ‘his heart’, with ἀκούοντος agreeing with τοῦ, ‘as he heard’, and ὠρίνετο the imperfect passive of ὀρίνω ‘stir, rouse’. βῆ δ’ ἰέναι is ‘and he set out to go’, an aorist with an infinitive, a common way of saying that someone started off. χροῒ is the dative of χρώς ‘skin, body’. ἔντε’ (ἔντεα) is ‘gear’, the house rendering, and ἐδύσετο is the aorist middle of δύω ‘put on’, with παμφανόωντα ‘all-shining’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὃ μὲν Αἰτωλοῖσιν ἀπήμυνεν κακὸν ἦμαρ
εἴξας ᾧ θυμῷ·
sentences.l:
So he for the Aetolians warded off the evil day,
yielding to his own heart;
sentences.i: So he warded off the evil day from the Aetolians, yielding to his own heart.
sentences.n: ὣς ὃ μέν ‘so he, for his part’ ends the story, with τῷ δέ in the next unit as the contrast. ἀπήμυνεν is the aorist of ἀπαμύνω ‘ward off from’, taking the dative Αἰτωλοῖσιν ‘from the Aetolians’ and κακὸν ἦμαρ ‘the evil day’, the day of the city’s fall. εἴξας ᾧ θυμῷ is ‘yielding to his own heart’ (εἴκω takes the dative; ᾧ is the possessive ὅς ‘his own’).

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ οὐκέτι δῶρα τέλεσσαν
πολλά τε καὶ χαρίεντα, κακὸν δ’ ἤμυνε καὶ αὔτως.
sentences.l:
but to him they no longer paid the gifts,
many and graceful, and he warded off the evil even so.
sentences.i: But they no longer gave him the gifts, the many graceful gifts; he warded off the evil even so, without them.
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘to him’, and δῶρα τέλεσσαν is ‘paid the gifts’ (τελέω ‘pay, fulfil’; the gifts had been promised at 576). πολλά τε καὶ χαρίεντα is ‘many and graceful’ (χαρίεις ‘graceful, pleasing’). κακὸν ἤμυνε καὶ αὔτως is ‘he warded off the evil even so’, αὔτως being ‘just so’, without the gifts. Meleager got no gifts because he had waited: this is the warning that Phoenix applies to Achilles in 604–605.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μή μοι ταῦτα νόει φρεσί, μὴ δέ σε δαίμων
ἐνταῦθα τρέψειε φίλος·
sentences.l:
But you, do not think these things in your wits for me, nor let a divinity
turn you that way, dear friend;
sentences.i: But do not let your mind run so, for my sake, and let no divinity turn you that way, my friend;
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ σύ μή … νόει is a present imperative with μή, ‘do not go on thinking’; μοι is an ethic dative, ‘for me, I ask’; ταῦτα ‘these things’ is Meleager’s course, to wait for the fire. μὴ δέ … τρέψειε is a wish with the aorist optative, ‘let (it) not turn you’; δαίμων is ‘a divinity’, an unnamed power that bends a man; ἐνταῦθα is ‘in that direction’. φίλος is taken as the vocative ‘dear friend’ (though the usual vocative is φίλε), closing the clause, and not as an epithet of δαίμων.

sentences.t:
κάκιον δέ κεν εἴη
νηυσὶν καιομένῃσιν ἀμυνέμεν·
sentences.l:
and it would be worse
to defend ships when they are burning;
sentences.i: and it would be worse to defend the ships once they are burning;
sentences.n: κάκιον ‘worse’ (the comparative of κακός) goes with κεν εἴη ‘it would be’; ἀμυνέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἀμύνω, ‘to defend’, with the dative νηυσὶν καιομένῃσιν ‘ships (when) burning’. The argument is about timing: better to act now, for gifts, than later among the flames; the fire of 436 is the danger Phoenix has already pictured.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ δώρων
ἔρχεο·
sentences.l:
but for the gifts
go;
sentences.i: No, go for the gifts;
sentences.n: ἐπὶ δώρων ἔρχεο is read ‘go for the gifts’, that is, on the strength of the gifts offered; the force of ἐπί with the genitive here is hard to pin down. ἔρχεο is the imperative of ἔρχομαι, with the epic ending -εο. ἀλλά ‘but’ sets this against the worse course of the last unit.

sentences.t: ἶσον γάρ σε θεῷ τίσουσιν Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l: for equally to a god will they honour you, the Achaeans.
sentences.i: for the Achaeans will honour you as they would a god.
sentences.n: ἶσον … θεῷ is ‘equally with a god’ (ἶσος takes the dative; ἶσον is adverbial). τίσουσιν is the future of τίω ‘honour’, the verb of 1.508; the form could also come from τίνω ‘pay’, but ‘honour’ is the sense that fits θεῷ. Ἀχαιοί are the army, who will honour Achilles as a god if he takes the gifts and fights.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κ’ ἄτερ δώρων πόλεμον φθισήνορα δύῃς
οὐκέθ’ ὁμῶς τιμῆς ἔσεαι πόλεμόν περ ἀλαλκών.
sentences.l:
But if without gifts the man-wasting war you enter,
no longer equally in honour will you be, even though you ward off the war.”
sentences.i: But if you enter the war that wastes men without the gifts, you will no longer be held in the same honour, even if you keep the war away.”
sentences.n: εἰ δέ κ’ … δύῃς is ‘but if you enter’: δύῃς is the aorist subjunctive of δύω in the sense ‘go into (the war)’, and ἄτερ δώρων is ‘without gifts’ (ἄτερ takes the genitive). φθισήνορα is ‘man-wasting’ (‘that wastes men’ in the free line). οὐκέθ’ ὁμῶς τιμῆς ἔσεαι is ‘you will no longer be equally of honour’ (a genitive of respect, ‘in point of honour’; ἔσεαι = ἔσῃ, the epic future of εἰμί), and πόλεμόν περ ἀλαλκών is ‘even if you ward off the war’ (ἀλαλκών is the aorist participle of ἀλέξω). This closes Phoenix’s speech; the edition prints no quotation marks, so the closing mark is ours.
